sections.normalized_html:
A quadratic equation has no real roots if the discriminant is negative: [MATH: \mathcal{D} < 0.]

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

[MATH: a = 2, \qquad b = q, \qquad c = 50]

So, computing the discriminant, we get

[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = (q)^{2} − 4(2)(50); = q^{2} − 400.]

To have no real solutions, we need [MATH: \mathcal{D} < 0{:}]

[MATH: q^{2} − 400|< 0; q^{2}|< 400; sqrt(q^{2})|< sqrt(400);|q||< 20; − 20 < q|< 20]

Since [MATH: q] must be an integer, we conclude that the least possible value is [MATH: -19.]

sections.normalized_html:
For a quadratic equation [MATH: ay^2 + by + c = 0,] the discriminant is [MATH: \mathcal{D} = b^2 - 4ac.]

  • If [MATH: \mathcal{D} > 0,] there are two distinct real solutions.

  • If [MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0,] there is one real solution.

  • If [MATH: \mathcal{D} < 0,] there are no real solutions (the solutions are complex).

First, rewrite the given equation in standard form:

[MATH: 3y^{2} + 6y - k = 0]

We have [MATH: a = 3], [MATH: b = 6], and [MATH: c = -k.]

Computing the discriminant, we get

[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = 6^{2} − 4(3)(− k); = 36 + 12k.]

For no real solutions, we require [MATH: \mathcal{D} < 0{:}]

[MATH: 36 + 12k|< 0; 12k|< − 36; k|< − 3]

So, any [MATH: k] less than [MATH: -3] would work.
Notice that among the given options, only [MATH: -4] is less than [MATH: -3.]

Therefore, [MATH: k = -4] is the correct answer.

sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: x(px - 24) = -9,] where [MATH: p] is an integer constant, has no real solutions, what is the least possible value of [MATH: p?]

sections.normalized_html:
A quadratic equation has no real solutions if the discriminant is negative: [MATH: \mathcal{D} < 0.]

First, rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form:

[MATH: x(px − 24)|= − 9; px^{2} − 24x|= − 9; px^{2} − 24x + 9|= 0]

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

[MATH: a = p, \qquad b = -24, \qquad c = 9]

So, computing the discriminant, we get

[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = (− 24)^{2} − 4(p)(9); = 576 − 36p.]

To have no real solutions, we need [MATH: \mathcal{D} < 0{:}]

[MATH: 576 − 36p|< 0; − 36p|< − 576; p|> (− 576)/(− 36); p|> 16]

Since [MATH: p] must be an integer, we conclude that the least possible value is [MATH: 17.]
